_note: Human values transcribed by the backend session on 2026-10-24 from Bigoni, Fridolfsson, Le Coq and Spagnolo, Fines, Leniency and Rewards in Antitrust: An Experiment, IFN Working Paper 738, version 2 November 2011 (hackathon/private/sources/). FACTS candidates until the main session enters them. The published RAND 2012 version was not available; the 2011 version is the one revised for it.
source: Bigoni, Fridolfsson, Le Coq, Spagnolo (2011) IFN WP 738 (revised for RAND Journal of Economics 43(2), 2012); tables as numbered in the 2011 version

noreport._note: Rome only; Fine in Rome: cartel price 5.031 (Section 5.2.3)

rematch._note: Rome only, perfect stranger, 25 periods (Section 5.2.3, footnote 21)

city_span._note: Stockholm-versus-Rome span per measure: the 2011 version reports city values only in footnote 15 (first-period communication attempts: Fine 0.660 vs 0.708, Leniency 0.525 vs 0.219). The full city table is in the 2009 CEPR version (Table 8); not transcribed.

design.demand: q_i = a/(1+g) - p_i/(1-g^2) + g p_j/(1-g^2), a = 36, c = 0, g = 0.8; profits rounded to integers
design.both_report: half the fine each (Leniency and Reward)
design.cartel_rule: communication forms a cartel; it can be fined in every later period until detected or reported; detection dismantles it; rematching ends it
design.communication: round 1: minimum acceptable price in 0..12; round 2: price in [min of round 1, 12]; agreed price = minimum of round 2
design.steps: 1 communication decision, 2 communication, 3 pricing, 4 secret reports, 5 market prices and public reports (only if no secret report), 6 detection, 7 summary (number of reporters shown when fined); L-Faire skips 4 to 6
design.default_price: if no price was chosen within 30 seconds, the default price was so high that the profit was 0
design.end_rule: after the first 20 periods, the first 15 percent rematching event ends the experiment (also a 2.5 hour cap, never binding)
design.sessions: 16 to 32 subjects per session, 390 subjects, Stockholm (SSE) and Rome (Tor Vergata), 2007; periods 21 to 29; 5 trial periods; endowment 1000 points; 200 points = 1 EUR
design.tests: multilevel random intercept models (duopoly, session, city)

results_numbered.1: Cartel deterrence: Fine and particularly Leniency deter cartel formation (comm. attempts 0.835 > 0.566 > 0.377; formation 0.716 > 0.315 > 0.178)
results_numbered.2: Cartel detection: Leniency substantially increases detection through self-reports (0.092 < 0.507; Reward 0.937)
results_numbered.3: Cartel recidivism: Leniency reduces re-formation after conviction (close to 40 percent immediate re-formation in Fine, much less in Leniency)
results_numbered.4: Average prices: Fine raises prices (5.349 > 4.917), Leniency leaves them almost unchanged (4.845)
results_numbered.5: Cartel prices: Fine (6.144) and Leniency (7.024) raise cartel prices relative to L-Faire (4.971)
results_numbered.6: Price deviations: Fine (0.424) and Leniency (0.373) reduce deviations relative to L-Faire (0.564)
results_numbered.7: Cartel prices and public reports: cartel price Fine 5.031 vs NoReport 3.553 (Rome)
results_numbered.8: Public reports as altruistic punishment: public reports given only the rival deviated higher in ReMatch (0.324) than Fine (0.197)
results_numbered.reward: Reward: formation 0.220 (above Leniency), reports 0.937, deviations 0.782 (above L-Faire), average price 3.973 and cartel price 5.339 below L-Faire; no pair took turns reporting (footnote 24)
